question: What term describes the biological steps through which a pathogen establishes infection and causes tissue injury?
explanation: Pathogenesis refers to the exact cellular and molecular mechanisms that lead to the development of a disease lesion following microbial entry. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is host tissue destruction during an infection often more severe than the direct mechanical presence of the microbe?

options.A: Normal flora reacts violently by attacking host organs directly
options.B: Red blood cells actively rupture when encountering foreign DNA
options.C: The immune response and microbial toxins contribute heavily to the damage
options.D: Pathogens consume all available oxygen in the bloodstream immediately

explanation: Much of the pathology seen in infectious lesions is collateral damage caused by the body's own inflammatory defense mechanisms alongside pathogen-derived toxins. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: What type of bacterial toxin is an integral structural component of the outer cell wall of Gram-negative organisms?
explanation: Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides located within the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria that are released primarily when the cell lyses. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do microbial enzymes like collagenase contribute directly to the formation of a spreading tissue lesion?

options.A: By neutralizing circulating antibodies in the bloodstream
options.B: By dissolving extracellular matrix barriers to allow deeper invasion
options.C: By directly stimulating the production of protective scar tissue
options.D: By transforming normal cells into malignant neoplasms

explanation: Extracellular enzymes break down connective tissue structural proteins, stripping away barriers that would otherwise contain the localized infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which white blood cell type is the primary responder during the early acute phase of an infectious lesion?
explanation: Neutrophils are recruited in massive numbers to the site of acute infection to phagocytose pathogens and release microbicidal agents. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: What defines the structural core of an abscess within an acute infectious lesion?

options.A: Proliferating fibroblasts and new blood vessels
options.B: Unaltered collagen fibers and dense scar tissue
options.C: A dormant capsule of calcified mineral deposits
options.D: Purulent exudate and liquefied cellular debris

explanation: An abscess develops when tissue undergoes liquefactive necrosis due to intense neutrophil activity, creating a pocket of pus. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which primary immune cell type characterizes chronic inflammatory lesions and granulomas?
explanation: Macrophages, along with lymphocytes, dominate chronic inflammatory reactions and form the structural foundation of granulomas. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary biological purpose of forming a granuloma around a persistent infectious agent?

options.A: To trigger immediate systemic anaphylaxis and clear the body of blood
options.B: To wall off and contain an organism that the immune system cannot easily eliminate
options.C: To immediately dissolve surrounding bone and soft tissue for rapid drainage
options.D: To convert the infectious agent into a harmless nutrient source for the host

explanation: Granulomas act as biological containment units designed to prevent the systemic spread of intracellular pathogens that resist standard clearance. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: A tissue biopsy showing marked eosinophilia and fibrotic encapsulation around a multicellular organism is most characteristic of which type of infection?
explanation: Parasites, particularly helminths, characteristically trigger eosinophilic responses and subsequent fibrous capsule formation due to their large physical size. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following pathological features is most commonly associated with acute bacterial tissue lesions?
explanation: Pyogenic bacterial infections recruit large numbers of neutrophils, leading to liquefactive tissue destruction and pus accumulation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: A patient with an infected surgical wound develops a heart rate of 115 beats per minute and a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. What clinical implication do these findings suggest?

options.A: An allergic reaction to the prescribed surface dressing material
options.B: Systemic involvement and potential progression toward sepsis
options.C: Normal recovery as the local inflammatory lesion begins to heal
options.D: Localized pain requiring only immediate topical analgesic application

explanation: Elevated heart and respiratory rates in the setting of infection indicate systemic stress and early inflammatory systemic involvement that demands urgent evaluation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why is it clinically critical to obtain wound culture specimens before initiating broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing local skin irritation from the swab
options.B: To isolate the specific causative organism before medications alter microbial load
options.C: To accelerate the natural physical closure of the open tissue lesion
options.D: To ensure the laboratory bill is processed under the correct diagnostic code

explanation: Starting antibiotics prior to drawing cultures can suppress pathogen growth, resulting in false-negative lab results and hindering targeted drug selection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)
